findings.title: Adding abstract method order() to the CryptoProvider SPI breaks existing implementations
findings.body: The new `int order();` method is added to the public `CryptoProvider` SPI interface without a default implementation. CryptoProvider is a published extension point loaded via ServiceLoader (documented Keycloak crypto SPI), so any third-party or downstream implementation compiled against the previous interface will (a) no longer compile and (b) at runtime fail with AbstractMethodError as soon as `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` calls `CryptoProvider::order` in the comparator while sorting the loaded providers. Previously-working custom crypto providers are therefore completely broken by this change, not just the new ordering feature. The method should be declared as `default int order() { return 0; }` (or similar) to preserve source and binary compatibility of the SPI.

findings.title: Silent, order-tied provider selection removes the FIPS misconfiguration safeguard
findings.body: detectProvider previously threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath, which acted as a hard safety check against misconfigured deployments (most importantly a classpath accidentally containing both the non-FIPS DefaultCryptoProvider and FIPS1402Provider). Now it silently picks one and only logs ignored providers at debug level. Both DefaultCryptoProvider and FIPS1402Provider return order() == 200, so in a deployment that accidentally contains both, the winner is decided by ServiceLoader iteration order (classpath order), which can silently select the non-FIPS-approved provider in an environment intended to run in FIPS mode, with no warning at any noticeable log level. At minimum, equal-order providers should produce a warning, and the FIPS/non-FIPS collision should be handled deterministically or fail loudly as before.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JVM default keystore provider, violating the interface contract
findings.body: The CryptoProvider contract for `getBouncyCastleProvider()` is to return the BouncyCastle (or BCFIPS) security provider. This implementation instead returns the provider of `KeyStore.getDefaultType()` (typically the SUN provider). Any shared code path in keycloak-common/keycloak-core that obtains the provider via this method and relies on BC-specific services (algorithms, keystore types like BCFKS/PKCS12 via BC, etc.) will get a provider that does not provide them, resulting in confusing NoSuchAlgorithmException/KeyStoreException failures rather than a clear 'not supported' signal, or worse, subtly different cryptographic behavior. Unlike the other methods that clearly throw UnsupportedOperationException, this one silently returns something that does not match the documented contract.

findings.title: Dead code in concatenatedRSToASN1DER creates and discards two ASN1 encoders
findings.body: Lines 114-115 (`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger); ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);`) create two encoders, write the integers into them, and throw the results away; only the `writeDerSeq(...)` chain on lines 117-121 contributes to the returned value. The statements have no effect, allocate objects unnecessarily on every signature conversion (a hot path during JWT signature verification), and look like leftover debugging code that will confuse future readers.

findings.title: ECDSA tests use a single P-256 keypair for ES384/ES512 and never verify the DER signature
findings.body: The test generates one keypair with the JVM default curve (P-256) and reuses it for all three algorithms. For ES384/ES512 the concatenated r/s halves are zero-padded 32-byte values, so the tests never exercise values whose most significant byte within the target length is set, nor the truncation branch of integerToBytes for real 48/66-byte r/s values. Additionally, the test only checks the concat→DER→concat round trip; it never verifies that the DER produced by concatenatedRSToASN1DER is a valid ECDSA signature via Signature.verify with the public key, which is the actual purpose of the conversion. A bug producing a well-formed but value-incorrect DER encoding would only be caught indirectly. The tests should generate curve-appropriate keypairs (P-384, P-521) and assert Signature.verify(convertedSignature). There is also no test at all for the core mechanism of this PR: the ServiceLoader registration of AuthzClientCryptoProvider and the CryptoIntegration order()-based provider selection/priority logic.
